title: Check Photo Resolution After an 8 × 10 Crop
description: Check print resolution after an 8 × 10 crop. Work out the remaining pixels per inch and compare the saved photo with your lab’s requirements.
direct: Crop a portrait photo to 4:5 first, then divide the remaining pixels by 8 and 10 inches. At 300 pixels per inch, you need at least 2400 × 3000 pixels after the crop.
figureAlt: A portrait photograph beneath an open 4:5 print mat
figureCaption: AI-generated illustration. The mat shows what the print keeps. The outer image shows what can fall outside the crop.
cards.decision.heading: Use the pixels left after cropping
cards.decision.body: For an 8 × 10 print that fills the paper, the image needs the same shape. A file can look large enough before cropping and still fall below the lab’s target after you trim the edges.
sections.detail-1.heading: Work through a near-match
sections.detail-1.body: A 3000 × 3736 portrait can be cropped to 2988 × 3735 pixels at 4:5. Divide 2988 by 8 and 3735 by 10. Both give 373.5 pixels per inch, before any further trim.
sections.detail-2.heading: Check whether the lab crops again
sections.detail-2.body: A photo editor’s crop and a lab’s order preview can differ. Inspect both. Leave space near the edge where the lab warns that it may trim the print.
faqs.reader-1.heading: Can resampling add captured detail?
faqs.reader-1.body: Resampling creates pixels using existing data. Fine detail still depends on the source photo.
faqs.reader-2.heading: What if I need to keep all edges?
faqs.reader-2.body: Use borders or choose a paper shape closer to the original.

steps.step-1.text: Check your photo lab’s target and whether it adds any trim. Open the original in DPI: Photo Print Prep and choose 8 × 10 inches with the intended orientation.
steps.step-2.text: Confirm the crop with room for the subject’s edges. Check the resulting pixel dimensions against the lab target. For landscape, swap the width and height.
steps.step-3.text: Export a copy and read back its dimensions. If you need more captured detail, try a less aggressive crop with borders, a smaller print, or a higher-resolution original.
